text: Meteorological station, Antarctic Peninsula 1957: Wind patterns formed complete musical score over sixhour period. Composition matched symphony that premiered in Vienna three months later. Composer had never seen weather data.

Personal diary, merchant's daughter, Florence 1634: The plague doctor's mask contained seventeen different faces today. Father says I have fever dreams but the baker's son drew the same seventeen faces without seeing my journal.

Archaeological survey, Mesopotamia 2400 BCE: USB drive recovered with cuneiform adapter still attached. Contains inventory of ziggurats not yet constructed. Drive formatted in Sumerian base60. Data corrupted by centuries of prayer.

Hospital records, St. Bartholomew's London 1665: Patient admitted with symptoms of temporal displacement. Complained of missing the internet. Spoke fluent English with accent that won't develop until Australian colonization.

Geological survey, Triassic period 210 million BCE: Dinosaur trackways form perfect hexagonal pattern spanning 12 kilometers. Pattern matches urban street grid of Philadelphia, 1682 city plan. Tracks predate William Penn by 210 million year

Census enumeration, rural Vermont 1820: Household listed family of four plus the Tuesday that got lost. Enumerator noted Tuesday responds to questions, pays taxes, owns property deed dated for day that never occurred.

Weather station data, Antarctica 1957: Barometric readings spell out recipe for grandmother's cookies in Morse code. No grandmother stationed at base. Recipe calls for ingredients that don't exist. Cookies taste exactly like childhood.

Monastery scriptorium, Canterbury 1198: Illuminated manuscript margin depicts monk copying the same manuscript. Each successive copy shows the monk growing older. Final panel shows empty desk. Manuscript remains unfinished.
Coroner's examination, Salem 1672: Deceased claimed death was clerical error, attended own autopsy. Provided detailed commentary on procedure. Certificate filed posthumously in subject's handwriting.

Medical journal, Edinburgh 1847: Surgeon reported patient's appendix contained seventeen unopened letters addressed to people who wouldn't be born for another century. All letters bore yesterday's postmark.

Archaeological survey, Mesopotamia 2400 BCE: Excavation recovered clay tablet with USB port carved into cuneiform. Port accepts modern cables. When connected, displays star charts for constellations that won't exist until 2157 CE.

Census bureau filing cabinet, Detroit 1962: Drawer labeled Population: Unborn contains 847 completed forms. All signatures in same handwriting. Birth dates range from 1963 to 2089. Forms filled out in 1962 ink.

Railroad survey records, Montana Territory 1883: Track measurements show railway line extends 23 miles beyond its physical terminus. Survey crew followed theoretical rails on foot for six hours before turning back at impossibility's edge.

Biological survey, Amazon basin 1952: Botanist catalogued tree species that produces fruit exactly 24 hours before it flowers. Local guides refuse to eat fruit, claiming it tastes like next week's regrets.

Architectural survey, Venice 1456: Cathedral contains confessional booth that absolves sins not yet committed. Priest's logbook records 347 future transgressions. Most frequent: Will forget to feed the pigeons, Thursday.
